title: Shorting a coin after Upbit flags it with a warning: 49 cases, a small edge, and why I only trade it with a 15 percent stop
author: Tasty-Mammoth5321
selftext:
I have been testing event driven ideas on crypto perps for a while, mostly to find out what does not work. Most of them did not. One survived long enough that I let it trade with a very small live account, so here is what it is and how thin it is.    
The setup: Upbit (the big Korean exchange) sometimes marks a coin with a caution designation, or announces a delisting. These coins often get sold in the hours after. The rule I tested is simple. When the flag or the delisting announcement appears, open a short on the perpetual contract at once (within about 15 minutes), put a stop at 15 percent above entry, and close after 72 hours at the latest.    
Results so far, after fees: 49 cases, average about 3.8 percent per trade, t-statistic around 2.6. Split by time, the older half shows about 3.4 percent and the newer hold out half about 4.6. It is a small sample from a short history, so I treat it as a hint, not a result. In the live account it has fired twice: one trade closed at plus 4.6 percent and one at plus 2.6 percent. Two trades prove nothing about the edge, they only prove the plumbing works.    
Why the stop matters: without it these shorts have bad tails. Small coins can squeeze hard, and in a related test on Korean listing shorts the unstopped version was negative because of a few extreme squeezes, while the same trades with a 15 percent stop were mildly positive. So the whole thing depends on accepting a stop that is wide and on sizing small enough that a stop hit does not matter.    
What does not work, which saved me time: racing the listing itself. The move on a new Upbit listing is almost entirely in the first second, and with a public Telegram feed I arrive about two seconds late, so by then the average edge is gone. Shorting pumps on a generic screener also lost money after costs in 2860 events over 180 days. Plain news headlines from public channels with a one to five minute delay were close to zero.    
What I am still unsure about: the sample is tiny, there are probably some days where several cases cluster, and a coin that Upbit flags may already be moving on other exchanges before the announcement. I check the result by week as well as by trade for that reason.    
Rules I keep for myself: tiny size, stop always on, no averaging down, and no manual "revenge" trade after a loss. I lost a deposit once by doing exactly that, which is why the stop is set by code and not by me.    
Would be curious if anyone has traded Korean exchange flags or delistings on perps and saw squeezes I have not hit yet, or knows a cleaner way to size a short on a thin coin.

comments.author: CreativeHomer
comments.body: The feature I'd care about most is identifying dangerous token launches before they become a problem. Holder concentration, liquidity changes and suspicious wallet activity seem more useful than another screen full of buy signals. I use Moon for crypto price wagers and that's already enough speculation for me lol. With memecoins, I'd want tools that help avoid bad setups rather than encourage faster entries.

comments.author: filwu
comments.body: Since the thesis hinges on the 15% stop, I’d separate the 49 events by warning vs delisting and include worst adverse excursion plus actual stop-fill slippage (including any gaps or skipped fills). A nominal stop may not cap realized loss on a thin perp during a squeeze, so the average +3.8% and t-stat do not describe that tail. Grouping by event date and coin, as well as by trade, would also show whether several flags clustered in one market move.
